book.title: הַקּוֹסֵם מֵאֶרֶץ אוֹז
book.author: L. Frank Baum
book.key: Verbs show binyan and root. <u>Underlined</u> words are passive in meaning (pu'al, hof'al, pa'ul, and nif'al when it means “was …ed”). Gold tags are idioms. Red numbers mark sentences; the notes below each paragraph use the same numbers.
book.credit: English text: L. Frank Baum, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (1900), public domain. Hebrew translation, vowels, glosses and notes made with Claude for this edition, CC BY 4.0.

s.line: Dorothy lived in the midst of the great Kansas prairies, with Uncle Henry, who was a farmer, and Aunt Em, who was the farmer’s wife.
s.note: בְּלֵב = "in the heart of", the usual way to say "in the middle of" a place: בְּלֵב הָעִיר (right in the city center), בְּלֵב הַיָּם (out at sea). אִשְׁתּוֹ שֶׁל הַחַקְלַאי ("his wife, of the farmer") is a very common modern pattern: the possessive ending points ahead to the owner named after שֶׁל. You could also say אֵשֶׁת הַחַקְלַאי.

w: הָיָה צָרִיךְ|one had to|~impersonal: it was necessary
s.line: Their house was small, for the lumber to build it had to be carried by wagon many miles.
s.note: הָיָה צָרִיךְ + infinitive with no subject = "one had to / it had to be …". Hebrew often avoids the English passive this way: הָיָה צָרִיךְ לְהוֹבִיל = "(it) had to be hauled". הוֹבִיל also means "to lead": הַקְּבוּצָה מוֹבִילָה (the team is in the lead).

w: הָיוּ בּוֹ|it had|~lit. there were in it
s.line: There were four walls, a floor and a roof, which made one room;
s.note: אַרְבָּעָה קִירוֹת: קִיר is masculine, so it takes the number form ending in ה. The same goes for the next sentence: שְׁלוֹשָׁה אוֹ אַרְבָּעָה כִּסְאוֹת, because כִּסֵּא is masculine even though its plural ends in וֹת.

s.line: and this room contained a rusty looking cookstove, a cupboard for the dishes, a table, three or four chairs, and the beds.
Uncle Henry and Aunt Em had a big bed in one corner, and Dorothy a little bed in another corner.
s.note: "X had Y" is <t>לְ</t>X <t>הָיָה</t> Y, and the verb agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner. Here it is <t>הָיְתָה</t> because <t>מִטָּה</t> is feminine; with two beds it would be <t>הָיוּ</t>.

w: עֲלִיַּת גַּג|an attic|~lit. going-up of roof
s.line: There was no garret at all,
and no cellar—except a small hole dug in the ground, called a cyclone cellar,
s.note: נֶחְפַּר and נִקְרָא are nif'al, here the passive of pa'al: חָפַר dug → נֶחְפַּר was dug; קָרָא called → נִקְרָא was called (it also means "was read"). Baum writes "cyclone", the American word in his day for a tornado, so this edition says טוֹרְנָדוֹ. מִקְלָט = shelter, the everyday Israeli word for the bomb shelter in a building.

s.line: where the family could go in case one of those great whirlwinds arose,
s.note: לְמִקְרֶה שֶׁ = "in case", followed by the future: קַח מְעִיל לְמִקְרֶה שֶׁיֵּרֵד גֶּשֶׁם (take a coat in case it rains). A storm קָמָה "rises up" in Hebrew as in English.

s.line: mighty enough to crush any building in its path.
It was reached by a trap door in the middle of the floor, from which a ladder led down into the small, dark hole.
s.note: יָרְדוּ "they went down", with no subject, means "one went down". Hebrew often turns an English passive ("it was reached") into a plural verb with no subject. You will see this all the time: אוֹמְרִים שֶׁ… = "it is said that …".

s.line: When Dorothy stood in the doorway and looked around, she could see nothing but the great gray prairie on every side.
s.note: לֹא … שׁוּם דָּבָר חוּץ מִ… = "nothing but …". חוּץ מִ = except; the same word gives בַּחוּץ = outside. פֶּתַח = an opening or doorway; פָּתַח (same letters) = he opened.

s.line: Not a tree nor a house broke the broad sweep of flat country that reached to the edge of the sky in all directions.
s.note: נִמְשַׁךְ is the nif'al of מָשַׁךְ (pull). It means "stretched" or "went on, lasted": הַשִּׁעוּר נִמְשַׁךְ שָׁעָה (the lesson lasted an hour). נִמְשָׁךְ לְ… = attracted to. מֶרְחָב (expanse) and רָחָב (wide) share the root ר־ח־ב.

s.line: The sun had baked the plowed land into a gray mass, with little cracks running through it.
s.note: הָפַךְ אֶת X לְ… = turned X into …. חָרוּשׁ (plowed) is a pa'ul participle of חָרַשׁ (to plow). Without vowels, חרש can also be חֵרֵשׁ "deaf". Watch for it at the end of the chapter.

s.line: Even the grass was not green, for the sun had burned the tops of the long blades until they were the same gray color to be seen everywhere.
s.note: אוֹתוֹ צֶבַע = "the same color": before a noun, אוֹתוֹ / אוֹתָהּ / אוֹתָם means "the same": בְּאוֹתוֹ יוֹם (on the same day). קְצוֹת is the construct plural of קָצֶה (edge, tip), as in קְצֵה הַשָּׁמַיִם above.

s.line: Once the house had been painted,
s.note: צָבוּעַ (painted) is a pa'ul participle of צָבַע (to paint), from the same root as צֶבַע (paint, color). פַּעַם at the start of a sentence = "once, at one time".

s.line: but the sun blistered the paint and the rains washed it away,
and now the house was as dull and gray as everything else.
When Aunt Em came there to live she was a young, pretty wife.
s.note: אִשָּׁה means both "woman" and "wife"; אִשְׁתּוֹ = his wife. גָּר = to live somewhere (אֵיפֹה אַתָּה גָּר?), while חַי = to be alive.

s.line: The sun and wind had changed her, too.
s.note: שִׁנָּה (pi'el) = to change something; הִשְׁתַּנָּה (hitpa'el) = to change, become different: הִיא הִשְׁתַּנְּתָה = she changed.

s.line: They had taken the sparkle from her eyes and left them a sober gray;
s.note: הֵן: שֶׁמֶשׁ and רוּחַ are both usually feminine, so "they" is הֵן. הִשְׁאִיר (hif'il) = to leave something; נִשְׁאַר (nif'al) = to stay, remain.

s.line: they had taken the red from her cheeks and lips, and they were gray also.
s.note: <t>לְחָיַיִם</t> (cheeks) and <t>שְׂפָתַיִם</t> (lips) are dual forms for things that come in pairs, like <t>עֵינַיִם</t>. <t>אֹדֶם</t> = redness; it is also the word for lipstick.

s.line: She was thin and gaunt, and never smiled now.

When Dorothy, who was an orphan, first came to her, Aunt Em had been so startled by the child’s laughter that she would scream and press her hand upon her heart whenever Dorothy’s merry voice reached her ears;
s.note: נִבְהַל מִ… (nif'al) = to get a fright from …; הִבְהִיל (hif'il) = to frighten someone: הַצְּחוֹק הִבְהִיל אוֹתָהּ = the laughter frightened her. לָרִאשׁוֹנָה = for the first time.
הָיְתָה צוֹרַחַת = "she would scream, used to scream". הָיָה + present participle describes a repeated habit in the past: בַּקַּיִץ הָיִינוּ הוֹלְכִים לַיָּם (in summer we used to go to the beach).

s.line: and she still looked at the little girl with wonder that she could find anything to laugh at.
s.note: הִתְפַּלֵּא (hitpa'el) = to be amazed; פֶּלֶא = a wonder, נִפְלָא = wonderful. Inside reported thought Hebrew keeps the present מוֹצֵאת ("finds"), where English shifts to "could find".

s.line: Uncle Henry never laughed.

w: מִבֹּקֶר עַד לַיְלָה|from morning till night|~fixed phrase
s.line: He worked hard from morning till night and did not know what joy was.
s.note: קָשֶׁה "hard" works as an adverb with no change: עָבַד קָשֶׁה = worked hard. מִבֹּקֶר עַד לַיְלָה = from morning till night, a fixed phrase. מַה זֹּאת שִׂמְחָה uses זֹּאת because שִׂמְחָה is feminine; in speech many people just say מַה זֶּה.

s.line: He was gray also, from his long beard to his rough boots,
s.note: Without vowels, זקן is both זָקָן (a beard) and זָקֵן (old, an old man). Context decides: לְסַבָּא יֵשׁ זָקָן (Grandpa has a beard) vs סַבָּא זָקֵן (Grandpa is old).

s.line: and he looked stern and solemn, and rarely spoke.
s.note: לְעִתִּים רְחוֹקוֹת = rarely, and its opposite לְעִתִּים קְרוֹבוֹת = often ("at near times"). Both are standard in modern writing; in speech you also hear לִפְעָמִים (sometimes) and הַרְבֵּה פְּעָמִים (often).

s.line: It was Toto that made Dorothy laugh, and saved her from growing as gray as her other surroundings.
s.note: הִצְחִיק is the hif'il (causative) of צָחַק: "to make someone laugh". מַצְחִיק = funny. Hif'il also makes "turn a color" verbs: הֶאֱפִיר (turn gray), הֶאֱדִים (turn red, blush), הֶחֱוִיר (turn pale). טוֹטוֹ הוּא שֶׁ… = "it was Toto who …", a way to stress one person.

s.line: Toto was not gray;
he was a little black dog,

w: הָיָה לוֹ|he had|~lit. there was to him
s.line: with long silky hair and small black eyes that twinkled merrily on either side of his funny, wee nose.
s.note: קְטַנְטַן = tiny, made by repeating the last syllable of קָטָן. The same pattern gives יְרַקְרַק (greenish) and אֲדַמְדַּם (reddish). בְּעַלִּיזוּת = בְּ + a noun is a common way to make an adverb: "with merriment" = merrily.

s.line: Toto played all day long, and Dorothy played with him, and loved him dearly.
s.note: כָּל הַיּוֹם (with הַ) = all day long; כָּל יוֹם (without it) = every day. The same with כָּל הַשָּׁבוּעַ (the whole week) vs כָּל שָׁבוּעַ (every week).

s.line: Today, however, they were not playing.
s.note: Hebrew has no continuous tense: <t>שִׂחֲקוּ</t> is both "played" and "were playing", and context decides.

s.line: Uncle Henry sat upon the doorstep and looked anxiously at the sky, which was even grayer than usual.
s.note: הִבִּיט בְּ… = to look at, with בְּ. שָׁמַיִם is plural in Hebrew, so שֶׁהָיוּ אֲפֹרִים is plural too. מֵהָרָגִיל = than usual: הַיּוֹם חַם מֵהָרָגִיל (it's hotter than usual today).

w: עַל הַיָּדַיִם|in her arms|~lit. on the hands
s.line: Dorothy stood in the door with Toto in her arms, and looked at the sky too.
s.note: עַל הַיָּדַיִם = held in someone's arms, as you would carry a baby: הִיא הֶחֱזִיקָה אֶת הַתִּינוֹק עַל הַיָּדַיִם. הִסְתַּכֵּל takes בְּ or עַל; both are fine.

s.line: Aunt Em was washing the dishes.
s.note: לִשְׁטֹף כֵּלִים = to wash the dishes; a dishwasher is a מֵדִיחַ כֵּלִים. כֵּלִים by itself means dishes, utensils or tools: כְּלֵי עֲבוֹדָה (work tools).

s.line: From the far north they heard a low wail of the wind,
and Uncle Henry and Dorothy could see where the long grass bowed in waves before the coming storm.
s.note: After verbs like רָאָה and שָׁמַע, Hebrew uses the present for what was going on at that moment: רָאוּ אֵיךְ הָעֵשֶׂב מִתְכּוֹפֵף = "saw the grass bending". הִתְקָרֵב (hitpa'el, from קָרוֹב "near") = to come closer.

s.line: There now came a sharp whistling in the air from the south,
s.note: נִשְׁמַע (nif'al) = was heard, the passive of שָׁמַע. In the present it also means "sounds": זֶה נִשְׁמָע טוֹב (that sounds good), and the everyday greeting מַה נִּשְׁמָע? (how are things?) is literally "what is heard?".

s.line: and as they turned their eyes that way they saw ripples in the grass coming from that direction also.
s.note: הִפְנָה (hif'il) = to turn something toward: הִפְנָה אֶת הַמַּבָּט (turned his gaze). פָּנָה (pa'al) = to turn oneself, as in פְּנֵה יָמִינָה (turn right), the voice of every navigation app.

s.line: Suddenly Uncle Henry stood up.
s.note: קָם = got up, stood up (also "woke up": קַמְתִּי בְּשֶׁבַע). עָמַד = was standing.

s.line: “There’s a cyclone coming, Em,” he called to his wife.
s.note: בַּדֶּרֶךְ = on the way: אֲנִי בַּדֶּרֶךְ (I'm on my way). קָרָא לְ… = called out to someone. קָרָא alone also means "read", and קָרְאוּ לוֹ … = "he was named …".

s.line: “I’ll go look after the stock.”
s.note: דָּאַג לְ… = to take care of, see to: אֲנִי אֶדְאַג לַכַּרְטִיסִים (I'll take care of the tickets). Without לְ, דָּאַג = to worry, as in בִּדְאָגָה (anxiously) above. בְּהֵמוֹת = farm animals, livestock.

s.line: Then he ran toward the sheds where the cows and horses were kept.
s.note: לְעֵבֶר = toward, a little more formal than לְכִוּוּן; you hear it in news reports: טִיל נוֹרָה לְעֵבֶר … (a missile was fired toward …). הֶחְזִיקוּ with no subject again stands for an English passive ("were kept").

w: עָזְבָה הַכֹּל|dropped everything|~idiom: lit. left everything
s.line: Aunt Em dropped her work and came to the door.
s.note: עָזַב הַכֹּל = dropped everything. Careful: עָזַב אֶת הָעֲבוֹדָה would mean "quit her job".

s.line: One glance told her of the danger close at hand.
s.note: הִסְפִּיק = was enough (זֶה מַסְפִּיק = that's enough), and also "managed in time": לֹא הִסְפַּקְתִּי לֶאֱכֹל = I didn't get a chance to eat.

s.line: “Quick, Dorothy!” she screamed.
“Run for the cellar!”
s.note: רוּצִי is the imperative to a woman or girl (רוּץ to a man, רוּצוּ to a group). מַהֵר is the masculine imperative of מִהֵר (to hurry), but it is used for anyone as the adverb "quickly".

s.line: Toto jumped out of Dorothy’s arms and hid under the bed, and the girl started to get him.
s.note: מִתַּחַת לְ… = under, and it needs לְ: מִתַּחַת לַמִּטָּה, מִתַּחַת לַשֻּׁלְחָן. נִגַּשׁ is nif'al with an active meaning, "to go up to, approach"; נִגַּשׁ לְמִבְחָן = to sit an exam.

s.line: Aunt Em, badly frightened, threw open the trap door in the floor and climbed down the ladder into the small, dark hole.
s.note: מְבֹהָל (pu'al participle) = frightened, a state. Compare נִבְהַל (nif'al, got a fright) and הִבְהִיל (hif'il, frightened someone). בְּבַת אַחַת = all at once, in one go. יָרַד בַּסֻּלָּם = went down by the ladder.

s.line: Dorothy caught Toto at last and started to follow her aunt.
When she was halfway across the room there came a great shriek from the wind,
s.note: <t>צָרְחָה צְרִיחָה</t>: a verb with a noun from the same root, as in <t>קָד קִידָה</t>.

w: אִבְּדָה אֶת שִׁוּוּי הַמִּשְׁקָל|lost her balance|~idiom: lit. lost the equality of weight
s.line: and the house shook so hard that she lost her footing and sat down suddenly upon the floor.
s.note: אִבֵּד אֶת שִׁוּוּי הַמִּשְׁקָל = lost one's balance (שִׁוּוּי מִשְׁקָל = balance). מָצָא אֶת עַצְמוֹ = found himself (somewhere, doing something), just as in English: מָצָאתִי אֶת עַצְמִי בְּתֵל אָבִיב.

s.line: Then a strange thing happened.
s.note: Without vowels, קרה is קָרָה "happened" (מָה קָרָה? = what happened?) and also קָרָה "cold" (feminine of קַר): מְנָה קָרָה = a cold dish.

s.line: The house whirled around two or three times and rose slowly through the air.
s.note: פַּעֲמַיִם = twice, a dual form of פַּעַם (time, occasion). פַּעַם is feminine, so "three times" is שָׁלוֹשׁ פְּעָמִים. לְאַט לְאַט = slowly, little by little; לְאַט alone = slowly.

w: בְּכַדּוּר פּוֹרֵחַ|in a balloon|~lit. a flying ball
s.line: Dorothy felt as if she were going up in a balloon.
s.note: כְּאִלּוּ = as if, followed by an ordinary verb, here the present עוֹלָה. In teenage speech it is also a filler, like English "like". כַּדּוּר פּוֹרֵחַ = hot-air balloon; פּוֹרֵחַ usually means "blooming", but פָּרַח can also mean "flew".

s.line: The north and south winds met where the house stood, and made it the exact center of the cyclone.
s.note: נִפְגַּשׁ is nif'al with a "each other" meaning: נִפְגְּשׁוּ = met (each other). נִפְגַּשְׁנוּ בַּקָּפֶה = we met at the café; פְּגִישָׁה = a meeting. מְדֻיָּק = exact, precise; בְּדִיּוּק = exactly.

w: בְּדֶרֶךְ כְּלָל|generally|~idiom: lit. in the general way
s.line: In the middle of a cyclone the air is generally still,

w: יוֹתֵר וְיוֹתֵר|higher and higher|~lit. more and more
s.line: but the great pressure of the wind on every side of the house raised it up higher and higher, until it was at the very top of the cyclone;
s.note: הֵרִים (hif'il) = to lift something; הִתְרוֹמֵם (hitpa'el, a few sentences back) = to rise by itself. לַחַץ = pressure, and in everyday speech also stress: אֲנִי בְּלַחַץ = I'm stressed. מַמָּשׁ = really, right (מַמָּשׁ פֹּה = right here).

s.line: and there it remained and was carried miles and miles away as easily as you could carry a feather.
s.note: נִשָּׂא (nif'al) = was carried, the passive of נָשָׂא (to carry). The same root gives נָשׂוּי (married) and נוֹשֵׂא (a topic). Note נִשְׁאַר just before it: nif'al again, but with an active meaning, "remained".

w: חֹשֶׁךְ מִצְרַיִם|pitch dark|~idiom: lit. Egypt's darkness
s.line: It was very dark, and the wind howled horribly around her,
s.note: חֹשֶׁךְ מִצְרַיִם = pitch dark, from the plague of darkness in the Exodus story, and still common today. בְּצוּרָה + adjective is a modern way to make an adverb: בְּצוּרָה נוֹרָאִית = horribly.

s.line: but Dorothy found she was riding quite easily.
s.note: דַּוְקָא = "actually, contrary to what you'd expect". It is one of the most typical words of spoken Hebrew: הַסֶּרֶט הָיָה דַּוְקָא טוֹב (the film was actually good).

s.line: After the first few whirls around, and one other time when the house tipped badly, she felt as if she were being rocked gently, like a baby in a cradle.
s.note: מְנַדְנְדִים אוֹתָהּ "(they) rock her" with no subject = "she is being rocked". נִדְנֵד = to rock or swing; a playground swing is a נַדְנֵדָה. In slang נִדְנֵד also means "to nag".

w: מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי|pleased|~idiom: lit. found favor in the eyes of
s.line: Toto did not like it.
s.note: מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי = "to please", the everyday way to say "like": הַסֶּרֶט מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינַי = I liked the film. The thing liked is the subject, and the person who likes it comes after בְּעֵינֵי.

w: פַּעַם לְכָאן וּפַעַם לְשָׁם|now here, now there|~idiom
בְּקוֹל רָם|loudly|~lit. in a high voice
s.line: He ran about the room, now here, now there, barking loudly;
s.note: בְּקוֹל רָם = loudly, out loud: לִקְרֹא בְּקוֹל רָם = to read aloud. פַּעַם … וּפַעַם … = "now …, now …".

s.line: but Dorothy sat quite still on the floor and waited to see what would happen.
s.note: Hebrew keeps the future יִקְרֶה ("will happen") where English says "would happen". זָז = to move; זוּז! = move! (get out of the way).

w: לְדֶלֶת הָרִצְפָּה|to the trap door|~lit. the floor door
s.line: Once Toto got too near the open trap door, and fell in;
s.note: פָּתוּחַ is the pa'ul (passive) participle of פָּתַח: "opened", so "open". Its opposite is סָגוּר (closed), which has the same pattern. Both are on every shop door.

s.line: and at first the little girl thought she had lost him.
s.note: אִבֵּד (pi'el) = to lose something. The thing itself נֶאֱבַד (nif'al, got lost), and הָלַךְ לְאִבּוּד = went missing.

s.line: But soon she saw one of his ears sticking up through the hole,
s.note: בּוֹלֵט = sticking out, and also "prominent, striking": הֶבְדֵּל בּוֹלֵט (a striking difference).

w: כָּךְ שֶׁהוּא|so that he|~כָּךְ שֶׁ־ = so that
s.line: for the strong pressure of the air was keeping him up so that he could not fall.
s.note: חָזָק (strong) and הֶחְזִיק (hif'il, to hold or keep) share the root ח־ז־ק. תַּחְזִיק מַעֲמָד! = hang in there! לַחַץ = pressure, and also stress: אֲנִי בְּלַחַץ = I'm stressed.

s.line: She crept to the hole, caught Toto by the ear, and dragged him into the room again,

w: כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא|so that no|~כְּדֵי שֶׁ־ + future = so that
s.line: afterward closing the trap door so that no more accidents could happen.
s.note: כְּדֵי שֶׁ־ takes the future tense even when the story is in the past: כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יִקְרוּ. תְּאוּנָה = accident; תְּאוּנַת דְּרָכִים = a road accident.

s.line: Hour after hour passed away, and slowly Dorothy got over her fright;
s.note: הִתְגַּבֵּר עַל = to overcome or get over. It comes from the root of strength, ג־ב־ר, as in גִּבּוֹר (hero) and גֶּבֶר (man).

s.line: but she felt quite lonely, and the wind shrieked so loudly all about her that she nearly became deaf.
s.note: Hebrew uses חָזָק (strong) for "loud": תְּדַבֵּר יוֹתֵר חָזָק = speak up. הִתְחָרֵשׁ = to go deaf, from חֵרֵשׁ (deaf).

s.line: At first she had wondered if she would be dashed to pieces when the house fell again;
s.note: הִתְרַסֵּק = to crash or shatter. It's the word in the news for a plane crash: הַמָּטוֹס הִתְרַסֵּק. תָּהָה = to wonder; תְּהִיָּה = a question one is pondering.

w: כְּכָל שֶׁעָבְרוּ|as … passed|~כְּכָל שֶׁ־ = as (over time)
s.line: but as the hours passed and nothing terrible happened, she stopped worrying and resolved to wait calmly and see what the future would bring.
s.note: הֶחְלִיט (hif'il) = to decide; הַחְלָטָה = a decision, a word you see constantly in the news (הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה הֶחְלִיטָה). הֵבִיא = to bring, the hif'il of בָּא (to come): literally "to make come".

s.line: At last she crawled over the swaying floor to her bed, and lay down upon it;
s.note: נִשְׁכַּב (nif'al, active meaning) = to lie down, the action. שָׁכַב (pa'al) = to be lying, the state. מִתְנַדְנֵד = swaying or swinging; נַדְנֵדָה = a playground swing.

w: הָלַךְ אַחֲרֶיהָ|followed her|~lit. went after her
s.line: and Toto followed and lay down beside her.
In spite of the swaying of the house and the wailing of the wind, Dorothy soon closed her eyes and fell fast asleep.
s.note: נִרְדַּם (nif'al, active meaning) = to fall asleep. הִרְדִּים (hif'il) = to put to sleep, and also to anaesthetize. עָצַם עֵינַיִם is the verb for closing your eyes only; a door is סָגַר.
